claim: ADP-ribosylation (ADPr) is a posttranslational modification (PTM) of proteins that controls many cellular processes, including DNA repair, transcription, chromatin regulation and mitosis.
source: ADP-ribosylation (ADPr) is a posttranslational modification (PTM) of proteins that controls many cellular processes, including DNA repair, transcription, chromatin regulation and mitosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ADP-ribosylation's role in cellular processes.

claim: Serine ADP-ribosylation (Ser-ADPr) is a new form of ADPr that is attached to serine residues in target proteins.
source: We recently discovered a new form of ADPr that is attached to serine residues in target proteins (Ser-ADPr)
evidence: This is a discovery reported by the authors in their recent work, supported by citation to their previous research.

claim: Ser-ADPr is specifically made by PARP1/HPF1 and PARP2/HPF1 complexes.
source: showed that this PTM is specifically made by PARP1/HPF1 and PARP2/HPF1 complexes.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous research findings.

claim: Histone Ser-ADPr is reversible in cells during response to DNA damage.
source: In this work, we found by quantitative proteomics that histone Ser-ADPr is reversible in cells during response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative proteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ARH3/ADPRHL2 is capable of efficiently and specifically removing Ser-ADPr of histones and other proteins.
source: By screening for the hydrolase that is responsible for the reversal of Ser-ADPr, we identified ARH3/ADPRHL2 as capable of efficiently and specifically removing Ser-ADPr of histones and other proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ser-ADPr is a major PTM in cells after DNA damage.
source: We further showed that Ser-ADPr is a major PTM in cells after DNA damage and that this signalling is dependent on ARH3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: Ser-ADPr signalling is dependent on ARH3.
source: We further showed that Ser-ADPr is a major PTM in cells after DNA damage and that this signalling is dependent on ARH3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ARH3 knockout cells.

claim: ADP-ribosylation regulates DNA damage repair, transcription, translation, aging, stress responses, and microbial pathogenicity.
source: ADP-ribosylation (ADPr) is a chemical modification of macromolecules that regulates a wide variety of cellular processes, such as DNA damage repair, transcription, translation, aging, stress responses, microbial pathogenicity and many others (Gupte et al., 2017; Hottiger, 2015; Jankevicius et al., 2016; Palazzo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ADP-ribosylation modification reaction involves the transfer of the ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ onto the target molecule and the release of nicotinamide.
source: The modification reaction involves the transfer of the ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ onto the target molecule and the release of nicotinamide (Gupte et al., 2017; Langelier et al., 2012; Schreiber et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ADP-ribosylation mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The human genome encodes 17 members of the PARP family.
source: The human genome encodes 17 members of the PARP family, which are grouped into five distinct classes according to protein domain architecture and involvement in different cellular processes (Perina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The majority of PARPs can catalyse the addition of only one unit of ADP-ribose (mono-ADPr) onto target proteins.
source: The majority of these PARPs can catalyse the addition of only one unit of ADP-ribose (mono-ADPr; MAR; MARylation) onto target proteins (Bütepage et al., 2015; Kleine et al., 2008; Vyas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PARP1, PARP2, and Tankyrases can generate long chains of repeating ADP-ribose units on their protein targets (poly-ADPr).
source: However, several PARP family members such as PARP1, PARP2, and Tankyrases can generate long chains of the repeating ADP-ribose units on their protein targets (poly-ADPr; PAR; PARylation) (D'Amours et al., 1999; Gibson and Kraus, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several amino acids have been reported as acceptors of PARP-mediated modification, most commonly glutamate, but also aspartate, lysine, arginine and cysteine.
source: Several amino acids have been reported as acceptors of PARP-mediated modification; most commonly glutamate, but also aspartate, lysine, arginine and cysteine (Daniels et al., 2015; Gagné et al., 2015; Martello et al., 2016; Vyas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Serine was identified as an acceptor of ADPr modification by PARP1 and PARP2.
source: Most recently, we identified serine as an acceptor of ADPr modification by PARP1 and PARP2 (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Leidecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: HPF1 (Histone PARylation Factor 1) is responsible for introducing the shift in amino acid specificity to serine in PARP1/2.
source: We also discovered that the PARP1/2 interacting protein HPF1 (Histone PARylation Factor 1) is responsible for introducing this shift in amino acid specificity (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Gibbs-Seymour et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Mass spectrometry of human cells treated with DNA damaging agents revealed large numbers of serine ADP-ribosylation modifications across a variety of human proteins involved in regulation of genome stability, including histones and PARP1 itself.
source: Further analyses, by utilising mass spectrometry of human cells treated with DNA damaging agents, revealed large numbers of serine ADP-ribosylation (Ser-ADPr) modifications across a variety of human proteins involved in regulation of genome stability, including histones and PARP1 itself (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Bilan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mass spectrometry studies.

claim: PARG is the most well characterized enzyme in humans for PAR hydrolysis.
source: PAR glycohydrolase (PARG) is the most well characterized enzyme in humans for PAR hydrolysis, which utilises a macrodomain fold to bind ADPr and specifically cleaves the ribose–ribose bonds between the subunits of the PAR chains (Lin et al., 1997; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PARG utilises a macrodomain fold to bind ADPr and specifically cleaves the ribose–ribose bonds between the subunits of the PAR chains.
source: PAR glycohydrolase (PARG) is the most well characterized enzyme in humans for PAR hydrolysis, which utilises a macrodomain fold to bind ADPr and specifically cleaves the ribose–ribose bonds between the subunits of the PAR chains (Lin et al., 1997; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: ARH3 is able to degrade PAR chains on proteins.
source: ADP-ribosylhydrolase 3 (ARH3, also called ADPRHL2) is also able to degrade PAR chains on proteins, but features a different structural composition to PARG, and hydrolyses PAR less efficiently (Hatakeyama et al., 1986; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006; Oka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH3 features a different structural composition to PARG and hydrolyses PAR less efficiently than PARG.
source: ADP-ribosylhydrolase 3 (ARH3, also called ADPRHL2) is also able to degrade PAR chains on proteins, but features a different structural composition to PARG, and hydrolyses PAR less efficiently (Hatakeyama et al., 1986; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006; Oka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither PARG nor ARH3 were previously shown to be able to process a single unit of ADPr (mono-ADPr) attached to a protein.
source: However, neither PARG nor ARH3 were previously shown to be able to process a single unit of ADPr (mono-ADPr) attached to a protein (Oka et al., 2006; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TARG1, MACROD1, MACROD2 and ARH1 specifically cleave amino acid-linked ADPr moieties and do not degrade PAR chains.
source: This MARylation is instead regulated by a different suite of proteins that do not degrade PAR chains, but rather specifically cleave amino acid-linked ADPr moieties; terminal ADPr protein glycohydrolase (TARG1), MACROD1, MACROD2 and ARH1 (Barkauskaite et al., 2015; Feijs et al., 2013; Jankevicius et al., 2013; Mashimo et al., 2014; Rosenthal et al., 2013; Sharifi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: TARG1, MACROD1 and MACROD2 hydrolyse acidic residue (Asp/Glu) linked mono-ADPr.
source: TARG1, MACROD1 and MACROD2 have been shown to hydrolyse acidic residue (Asp/Glu) linked mono-ADPr, whilst ARH1 is capable of removing ADPr from arginine (Glowacki et al., 2002; Jankevicius et al., 2013; Rosenthal et al., 2013; Sharifi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH1 is capable of removing ADPr from arginine.
source: TARG1, MACROD1 and MACROD2 have been shown to hydrolyse acidic residue (Asp/Glu) linked mono-ADPr, whilst ARH1 is capable of removing ADPr from arginine (Glowacki et al., 2002; Jankevicius et al., 2013; Rosenthal et al., 2013; Sharifi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PARP-dependent ADP-ribosylation signalling is a rapid and dynamic process in human cells.
source: PARP-dependent ADP-ribosylation signalling is a rapid and dynamic process in human cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP signaling dynamics.

claim: Within minutes of incurring DNA damage, the peak PARylation signal is observed, before it quickly diminishes.
source: Within minutes of incurring DNA damage, the peak PARylation signal is observed, before it quickly diminishes (Figure 1A) (Hakmé et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2007; Tallis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All detected Ser-ADPr marks increased in cells exposed to oxidative DNA damage for 10 min.
source: As expected, all the detected Ser-ADPr marks increased in cells exposed to oxidative DNA damage for 10 min (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1) (Leidecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D and supplementary figures.

claim: After 120 min of H2O2 treatment, Ser-ADPr returned to levels similar to the untreated cells.
source: However, after 120 min of H2O2 treatment, Ser-ADPr returned to levels similar to the untreated cells (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1), demonstrating that Ser-ADPr is also a reversible modification.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D and supplementary figures.

claim: Only ARH3 was able to catalyse removal of ADPr from the histone peptide.
source: Strikingly, only ARH3 was able to catalyse removal of ADPr from the histone peptide, implicating a serine ADP-ribosylhydrolase activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the hydrolase screening assay.

claim: Both PARG and ARH3 were able to degrade the PAR chains on automodified PARP1.
source: As expected, we also observed that both PARG and ARH3 were able to degrade the PAR chains on automodified PARP1 (Figure 2A, lanes 2 and 8), albeit ARH3 was less efficient in removing the chains (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: ARH3 was less efficient than PARG in removing PAR chains.
source: As expected, we also observed that both PARG and ARH3 were able to degrade the PAR chains on automodified PARP1 (Figure 2A, lanes 2 and 8), albeit ARH3 was less efficient in removing the chains (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: ARH3 was able to remove both the PARylation and mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation of H1.
source: Whilst ARH3 was able to remove both the PARylation and mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation of H1, PARG was only able to degrade the PAR chains on histone H1 and PARP1, leaving a mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation signal that was visible as two distinct bands at the sizes of H1 and PARP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PARG was only able to degrade the PAR chains on histone H1 and PARP1, leaving a mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation signal.
source: Whilst ARH3 was able to remove both the PARylation and mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation of H1, PARG was only able to degrade the PAR chains on histone H1 and PARP1, leaving a mono(ADP-ribosyl)ation signal that was visible as two distinct bands at the sizes of H1 and PARP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most of the ADP-ribosylated chains had been attached to serine residues.
source: A double digestion with PARG/ARH3 confirmed that most of the ADP-ribosylated chains had been attached to serine residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from double digestion experiments shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The E988Q mutation alters the activity of PARP1 to that of mono-ADP-ribosylation.
source: The E988Q mutation alters the activity of PARP1 to that of mono-ADP-ribosylation, so in this way we were able to generate Ser mono-ADPr modifications on a protein target that is otherwise PARylated under wild type conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The serine mono-ADP-ribosylated histone H1 samples were only hydrolysed by ARH3.
source: However, the serine mono-ADP-ribosylated histone H1 samples were only hydrolysed by ARH3 (Figure 2C, lane 9), with no notable reduction in mono-ADP-ribose band intensity by the other hydrolases, including PARG.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All identified histone ADPr peptides were significantly decreased in samples treated with recombinant ARH3.
source: All the identified histone ADPr peptides were significantly decreased in samples treated with recombinant ARH3 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1), demonstrating that this hydrolase is also able to remove Ser-ADPr from endogenous histones.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ARH3 is able to remove Ser-ADPr from endogenous histones.
source: All the identified histone ADPr peptides were significantly decreased in samples treated with recombinant ARH3 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1), demonstrating that this hydrolase is also able to remove Ser-ADPr from endogenous histones.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative proteomics data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The isolated PARP1 automodification domain (aa 374-525) is modified on 3 serine residues when incubated in the presence of full length PARP1 and HPF1.
source: We have recently characterised the Ser-ADPr sites on the isolated automodifcation domain of PARP1 (aa 374-525) when incubated in the presence of full length PARP1 and HPF1 (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a). During this reaction, the isolated domain is modified on 3 serine residues
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: ARH3 was efficient at removing Ser-ADPr modifications from both the mono- and poly-ADP-ribosylated automodification domain.
source: ARH3 was efficient at removing Ser-ADPr modifications from both the mono- and poly-ADP-ribosylated automodification domain, confirming the capability to hydrolyse serine linked ADP-ribose from protein targets besides histones.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the hydrolase assay.

claim: ARH3 alone was sufficient for the complete removal of Ser-ADPr from H3 histone peptide in the absence of PARP1 and HPF1.
source: The autoradiogram demonstrated that ARH3 alone was sufficient for the complete removal of Ser-ADPr from H3 histone peptide in the absence of PARP1 and HPF1.
evidence: This is supported by autoradiogram data from the purified peptide assay.

claim: The purified ADP-ribosylated H2B peptide is efficiently and specifically de-ADP-ribosylated by ARH3.
source: Our previous study established that Ser6 of H2B is ADP-ribosylated by PARP1 in the presence of HPF1 (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a), and similarly as for H3, we could show that the purified ADP-ribosylated H2B peptide is efficiently and specifically de-ADP-ribosylated by ARH3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Asp77 and Asp78 are critical acidic amino acids required for coordination of a magnesium ion and poly(ADP-ribose) hydrolysis in ARH3.
source: Earlier research on ARH3 identified the critical acidic amino acids Asp77 and Asp78 that are required for coordination of a magnesium ion and poly(ADP-ribose) hydrolysis (Oka et al., 2006) (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only wild type ARH3 was able to remove the Ser-ADPr modification from the histone H3 and H2B peptides, while D77N, D78N, and D77N D78N mutants could not.
source: Only wild type ARH3 was able to remove the Ser-ADPr modification from the histone H3 and H2B peptides.
evidence: This is supported by data from mutant ARH3 experiments shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Asp77 and Asp78 are necessary for both PAR and serine-ADPr hydrolysis by ARH3.
source: These results show that Asp77 and Asp78 are necessary for both PAR and serine-ADPr hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant experiments showing loss of activity.

claim: In the presence of the metal chelating agent EDTA, ARH3 was unable to hydrolyse the substrate, confirming that the activity is Mg2+ dependent.
source: Further, in the presence of the metal chelating agent EDTA, ARH3 was unable to hydrolyse the substrate, confirming that the activity is Mg2+ dependent (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: ARH3 enzymatic activity is concentration and time dependent.
source: Furthermore, we showed that ARH3 enzymatic activity is concentration and time dependent (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: ARH3 was highly efficient against Ser-ADPr and quantitatively hydrolysed the substrate at nanomolar enzyme concentrations.
source: Notably, ARH3 was highly efficient against Ser-ADPr and quantitatively hydrolysed the substrate at nanomolar enzyme concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by concentration-dependent activity data.

claim: Both MACROD2 and TARG1, but not ARH1, nor ARH3, were able to catalyse the efficient removal of glutamate mono-ADP-ribose from the PARP1 protein.
source: The autoradiogram shows that both MACROD2 and TARG1, but not ARH1, nor ARH3, were able to catalyse the efficient removal of glutamate mono-ADP-ribose from the PARP1 protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only ARH1, but not ARH2, ARH3 or TARG1, efficiently cleaved the arginine ADP-ribosylated proteins in the cell extracts.
source: Figure 4B shows that only ARH1 (that was used as a positive control), but not ARH2, ARH3 or TARG1, efficiently cleaved the arginine ADP-ribosylated proteins in the cell extracts.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ARH3 and TARG1 showed no activity against lysine-linked ADPr on H3 peptide.
source: We observed no activity of ARH3, nor TARG1 against this substrate.
evidence: This is supported by data from the lysine-ADPr assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ARH3 is unable to catalyse the efficient removal of glutamate, arginine or lysine linked ADP-ribose moieties, and is specific for Ser-ADPr hydrolysis.
source: All together, these findings confirm that ARH3 is unable to catalyse the efficient removal of glutamate, arginine or lysine linked ADP-ribose moieties, and is specific for Ser-ADPr hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of specificity assays.

claim: ARH3 KO cells showed higher levels of ADP-ribosylated proteins under unstimulated conditions compared to control cells.
source: When compared to control cells, ARH3 KO cells showed higher levels of ADP-ribosylated proteins under unstimulated conditions.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ADP-ribosylation is dramatically induced in both wt and ARH3 KO cells following DNA damage.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, ADP-ribosylation is dramatically induced in both wt and ARH3 KO cells following DNA damage (see 10 min samples), particularly on PARP1 and Histone proteins.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 2 hr post DNA damage, in the ARH3 KO cells the ADPr signal persisted whilst in the wild type cells the ADPr signal was greatly reduced.
source: However, the difference between wt and ARH3 KO cells became dramatic at 2 hr post DNA damage, in the ARH3 KO cells the ADPr signal persisted whilst in the wild type cells the ADPr signal was greatly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The persistence of ADPr signal at 2 hr post DNA damage was most clear with the short oligo- and mono-ADPr as detected by pan-ADPr antibody.
source: This observation was most clear with the short oligo- and mono-ADPr as detected by pan-ADPr antibody, while turnover of long chains (see the signal at PARP1 detected by PAR antibody) was much less affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PARG is required in an early phase of DNA-damage response, shortening long chains of Ser-ADPr substrates, producing mono (and likely very short chains) which subsequently are substrates of ARH3 enzymatic activity.
source: This may suggest that PARG is required in an early phase of DNA-damage response, shortening long chains of Ser-ADPr substrates, producing mono (and likely very short chains) which subsequently are substrates of ARH3 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential effects on long vs short chains.

claim: ARH3 erases the persisting ADPr signal at 120 min post DNA damage when added to ARH3 KO extracts.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, ARH3 erases the persisting ADPr signal (at 120 min post DNA damage), confirming that ARH3 is both necessary and sufficient for removal of these modifications.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ARH3 is both necessary and sufficient for removal of ADPr modifications persisting at 120 min post DNA damage.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, ARH3 erases the persisting ADPr signal (at 120 min post DNA damage), confirming that ARH3 is both necessary and sufficient for removal of these modifications.
evidence: This is supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MACROD2 and PARG were not capable of hydrolysing the persisting ADPr substrates at 120 min post DNA damage when added to the extracts.
source: MACROD2 and PARG were not capable of hydrolysing the same substrates, when added to the extracts and probed with pan-ADPr, suggesting that accumulation of monoADPr was on serine residues (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The accumulation of monoADPr in ARH3 KO cells at 120 min post DNA damage was on serine residues.
source: MACROD2 and PARG were not capable of hydrolysing the same substrates, when added to the extracts and probed with pan-ADPr, suggesting that accumulation of monoADPr was on serine residues (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the hydrolases tested.

claim: After 120 min of DNA damage, the levels of histone Ser-ADPr were dramatically increased in ARH3 KO cells compared the wild type cells.
source: As expected, after 120 min of DNA damage, the levels of histone Ser-ADPr were dramatically increased in ARH3 KO cells compared the wild type cells. (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ARH3 completely removes ADPr from core histones derived from DNA damage treated cells.
source: Identically to what we observed for in vitro Ser-ADPr on peptides and proteins, ARH3 completely removes ADPr from core histones derived from DNA damage treated cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Histone ADPr is exclusively on serine residues under DNA damage experimental conditions.
source: This confirms our previous mass spectrometric analyses that conclusively identified histone ADPr on serine, but not other residues (Leidecker et al., 2016), thus providing further indication of serines as the exclusive modification sites on core histones under these experimental conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous mass spectrometry work and the ARH3 specificity data.

claim: Following a strong induction of histone Ser-ADPr after 10 min of treatment with peroxide, the modification is completely reversed after 120 min.
source: As expected, following a strong induction of histone Ser-ADPr after 10 min of treatment with peroxide, the modification is completely reversed after 120 min (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Disruption of the enzymes responsible for deconjugational (and conjugational) dynamics of PTMs often leads to disease states.
source: As with all homeostatic and stress control systems, this level of regulation relies on reversibility to maintain balance, in this case the fine-tuning of the attachment and removal of PTMs. In fact, disruption of the enzymes responsible for deconjugational (and conjugational) dynamics of PTMs often leads to disease states.
evidence: This is general knowledge about PTM regulation and disease.

claim: Disregulation of mono- or poly-ADPr processes can result in neurodegenerative disorders and cancer.
source: This also applies to ADP-ribosylation, as disregulation of mono- or poly-ADPr processes can result in neurodegenerative disorders and cancer (Bütepage et al., 2015; Hanai et al., 2004; Rouleau et al., 2010; Sharifi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nearly 300 hundred Ser-ADPr modification sites were identified in proteins extracted from living cells.
source: Our data identified nearly 300 hundred Ser-ADPr modification sites in proteins extracted from living cells, suggesting that this PTM is widespread across a breadth of pathways including; DNA repair, chromatin organisation, mitotic nuclear division, DNA recombination, transcriptional regulation and mRNA splicing amongst others (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Ser-ADPr is widespread across pathways including DNA repair, chromatin organisation, mitotic nuclear division, DNA recombination, transcriptional regulation and mRNA splicing.
source: Our data identified nearly 300 hundred Ser-ADPr modification sites in proteins extracted from living cells, suggesting that this PTM is widespread across a breadth of pathways including; DNA repair, chromatin organisation, mitotic nuclear division, DNA recombination, transcriptional regulation and mRNA splicing amongst others (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of modification sites in proteins involved in these pathways.

claim: At least a fraction of Ser-ADPr targets are modified by the HPF1/PARP1/2 complex, including histones, PARP1 itself and High Mobility Group (HMG) proteins.
source: We further showed that at least a fraction of these Ser-ADPr targets are modified by the HPF1/PARP1/2 complex, including histones, PARP1 itself and High Mobility Group (HMG) proteins, as we were able to reconstitute the sites in vitro using recombinant proteins (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Gibbs-Seymour et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work showing in vitro reconstitution.

claim: ARH3 has previously been demonstrated to cleave PAR chains, although less rapidly than PARG.
source: ARH3 has previously been demonstrated to cleave PAR chains, although less rapidly than PARG, but also to hydrolyse O-acetyl-ADP-ribose by-products generated by Sir2 deacetylases (Mashimo et al., 2013; Oka et al., 2006; Ono et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH3 hydrolyses O-acetyl-ADP-ribose by-products generated by Sir2 deacetylases.
source: ARH3 has previously been demonstrated to cleave PAR chains, although less rapidly than PARG, but also to hydrolyse O-acetyl-ADP-ribose by-products generated by Sir2 deacetylases (Mashimo et al., 2013; Oka et al., 2006; Ono et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH3 is capable of efficiently removing Ser-ADPr in a magnesium-dependent manner.
source: Here, we established that ARH3 is also capable of efficiently removing Ser-ADPr in a magnesium-dependent manner, and that mutation of key aspartate residues (which are also critical for PAR cleavage) ablates this activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of key aspartate residues (which are also critical for PAR cleavage) ablates ARH3's Ser-ADPr hydrolysis activity.
source: Here, we established that ARH3 is also capable of efficiently removing Ser-ADPr in a magnesium-dependent manner, and that mutation of key aspartate residues (which are also critical for PAR cleavage) ablates this activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutant ARH3 experiments.

claim: ARH3 protein possesses a mitochondrial targeting peptide at the N-terminus (both in Human and Murine proteins).
source: Prior observations suggest a wide distribution of ARH3 throughout the cell; cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria—an interesting array of localisations given that the ARH3 protein possesses a mitochondrial targeting peptide at the N-terminus (both in Human and Murine proteins) (Mashimo et al., 2013; Niere et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH3 has a wide distribution throughout the cell including cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria.
source: Prior observations suggest a wide distribution of ARH3 throughout the cell; cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria—an interesting array of localisations given that the ARH3 protein possesses a mitochondrial targeting peptide at the N-terminus (both in Human and Murine proteins) (Mashimo et al., 2013; Niere et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ARH3 functioned in the degradation of PAR chains that had been released by both nuclear and cytosolic PARG following the oxidative stress exposure.
source: Previous studies suggested that ARH3 functioned in the degradation of PAR chains that had been released by both nuclear and cytosolic PARG following the oxidative stress exposure.
evidence: This is based on previous studies about ARH3 function.

claim: ARH3 buffers the Parthanatos response (a Caspase-independent cell death induced by the transport and binding of PAR to mitochondrial protein AIF).
source: As a result of this cooperation, ARH3 buffers the Parthanatos response (a Caspase-independent cell death induced by the transport and binding of PAR to mitochondrial protein AIF) (Mashimo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: ARH3 KO MEFs were found to be sensitive to hydrogen peroxide compared to wild type cells.
source: Furthermore, ARH3 KO MEFs were found to be sensitive to hydrogen peroxide compared to wild type cells, and in the absence of ARH3 protein PAR was observed to accumulate in the nucleus (Mashimo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the absence of ARH3 protein PAR was observed to accumulate in the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, ARH3 KO MEFs were found to be sensitive to hydrogen peroxide compared to wild type cells, and in the absence of ARH3 protein PAR was observed to accumulate in the nucleus (Mashimo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The sensitivity of the ARH3 KO MEFs to hydrogen peroxide was rescued by treatment with a PARP1 inhibitor.
source: Additionally, the sensitivity of the ARH3 KO MEFs to hydrogen peroxide was rescued by treatment with a PARP1 inhibitor, linking the function of ARH3 to the PARP1 controlled DNA damage response (Mashimo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The ADP-ribose linked to serine via an O-glycosidic bond is chemically similar to the ribose-ribose bond within the ADP-ribose polymer.
source: The ADP-ribose linked to serine via an O-glycosidic bond is chemically similar to the ribose-ribose bond within the ADP-ribose polymer (Bonfiglio et al., 2017b; Leidecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing the chemical structure.

claim: PARG has a preference for binding to the long PAR chains and is inefficient in hydrolysing short oligo-ADPr fragments and incapable or removing mono-ADPr.
source: Both enzymes perform acid-base catalysis in PAR hydrolysis, but PARG has a preference for binding to the long PAR chains and is inefficient in hydrolysing short oligo-ADPr fragments and incapable or removing mono-ADPr (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Hatakeyama et al., 1986; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both PARG and ARH3 perform acid-base catalysis in PAR hydrolysis.
source: Both enzymes perform acid-base catalysis in PAR hydrolysis, but PARG has a preference for binding to the long PAR chains and is inefficient in hydrolysing short oligo-ADPr fragments and incapable or removing mono-ADPr (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Hatakeyama et al., 1986; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PARG adopts a macrodomain fold with a unique catalytic loop allowing for hydrolysis of ADPr.
source: Architecturally, both enzymes are clearly distinct from each other, with PARG adopting a macrodomain fold with a unique catalytic loop allowing for hydrolysis of ADPr, whilst ARH3 has an eponymous ARH fold featuring a binucleate Mg2+ catalytic site (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: ARH3 has an eponymous ARH fold featuring a binucleate Mg2+ catalytic site.
source: Architecturally, both enzymes are clearly distinct from each other, with PARG adopting a macrodomain fold with a unique catalytic loop allowing for hydrolysis of ADPr, whilst ARH3 has an eponymous ARH fold featuring a binucleate Mg2+ catalytic site (Barkauskaite et al., 2013; Mueller-Dieckmann et al., 2006; Slade et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Mass spectrometry has played an indispensable role in the discovery of Ser-ADPr as a widespread signal in DNA repair.
source: Advanced mass spectrometry has played an indispensable role in the discovery of Ser-ADPr as a widespread signal in DNA repair and in the identification of the enzymes and cofactors responsible for its attachment (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a; Leidecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous mass spectrometry work.

claim: ARH3 allows a simple exploration of histone Ser-ADPr dynamics during DNA damage response when used in combination with the anti-pan ADPr binding reagent.
source: In combination with available biological techniques and tools, such as the anti-pan ADPr binding reagent (Gibson et al., 2016), we showed that ARH3 allows a simple exploration of histone Ser-ADPr dynamics during DNA damage response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data demonstrating the use of ARH3 as a tool.

claim: Ser6 of H2B is ADP-ribosylated by PARP1 in the presence of HPF1.
source: Our previous study established that Ser6 of H2B is ADP-ribosylated by PARP1 in the presence of HPF1 (Bonfiglio et al., 2017a)
